clinicalPearls: Anomalous origin of the left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery (ALCAPA) means the left ventricular myocardium is perfused by desaturated pulmonary blood at low pressure once the pulmonary vascular resistance falls after birth.
The classic presentation is an infant in the first months of life with irritability, sweating and pallor during feeds, representing angina, often mistaken for colic.
As pulmonary pressure declines, flow reverses and the left coronary steals into the pulmonary trunk, producing a coronary steal that worsens ischaemia.
Collaterals from the right coronary artery determine survival; an adult type with rich collaterals may present late with a murmur, arrhythmia or sudden death.
The electrocardiogram typically shows an anterolateral infarction pattern with deep Q waves and ST-T changes in the lateral leads.
Echocardiography shows a dilated, poorly contracting left ventricle with mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle ischaemia, and retrograde colour flow into the pulmonary artery.
Surgical re-implantation of the anomalous coronary into the aorta to establish a dual coronary system is the definitive treatment.
Left ventricular function often recovers remarkably after successful revascularisation even when severely depressed preoperatively.
reference.pathophysiology: During fetal life the pulmonary arterial pressure and oxygen saturation are high, so a left coronary artery arising from the pulmonary trunk is adequately perfused. After birth the pulmonary vascular resistance and pressure fall, reducing antegrade perfusion pressure and oxygen delivery to the left coronary territory. The myocardium becomes progressively ischaemic, and once right-to-left coronary collaterals develop, blood flows from the higher-pressure right coronary system through collaterals into the left coronary and drains into the low-pressure pulmonary artery, a coronary steal. The result is chronic subendocardial ischaemia and infarction of the anterolateral left ventricle and papillary muscles, causing dilated cardiomyopathy and mitral regurgitation.
additionalDifferentials: anomalous left coronary from the right sinus with interarterial course
additionalInvestigations: transthoracic echocardiography with colour Doppler of the coronary origins
cardiac catheterisation and selective coronary angiography
CT or MR coronary angiography for origin and collateral mapping
serum cardiac troponin and B-type natriuretic peptide
chest radiograph for cardiomegaly and pulmonary congestion
redFlags: infant with episodic distress and sweating on feeding suggesting angina
signs of cardiogenic shock or heart failure in early infancy
electrocardiographic infarction pattern in an infant
syncope, ventricular arrhythmia or aborted sudden death in an older child
reference.prognosis: Untreated infantile ALCAPA carries a high mortality within the first year, but early surgical establishment of a two-coronary system yields excellent long-term survival and frequently full recovery of ventricular function.
pitfalls: Diagnosing idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy or myocarditis without interrogating the coronary origins on echocardiography.
Mislabelling feeding-related distress and sweating as colic or reflux.
Assuming normal coronaries because the left main appears to arise near the aorta without confirming true aortic origin and flow direction.
Underestimating mitral regurgitation as primary valve disease rather than ischaemic papillary muscle dysfunction.
Delaying referral in an older asymptomatic child with an incidental murmur and collateral-dependent perfusion.
references: Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics, current edition
Moss and Adams Heart Disease in Infants, Children, and Adolescents
AHA/ACC guideline on management of adults with congenital heart disease
management: Undertake urgent surgical re-establishment of a two-coronary system by re-implanting the anomalous left coronary artery into the aorta
Stabilise heart failure preoperatively with diuretics, inotropic and afterload-reducing support, and mechanical ventilation where required
Manage ischaemic mitral regurgitation expectantly, as it often improves after revascularisation, reserving valve repair for severe or persistent regurgitation
Monitor postoperatively for recovery of left ventricular function and residual myocardial ischaemia
Maintain long-term surveillance for arrhythmia and mitral valve function
Manage under a paediatric cardiology and cardiac surgery multidisciplinary team
